final_proof:
**Reading of the statement.** The statement has two evident typos, which we correct (these do not change the claim). Since $L:\mathbf D\to\mathbf C$, its opposite is $L^{\text{op}}:\mathbf D^{\text{op}}\to\mathbf C^{\text{op}}$, given by $L^{\text{op}}(D)=LD$ on objects and $L^{\text{op}}(f^{\text{op}})=(Lf)^{\text{op}}$ on morphisms. The hom bifunctor of $\mathbf C$ is $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(-,-):\mathbf C^{\text{op}}\times\mathbf C\to\mathbf{Set}$. Only with these domains and codomains is the composite $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(-,-)\circ(L^{\text{op}}\times\operatorname{id}_{\mathbf C})$ defined, since $L^{\text{op}}\times\operatorname{id}_{\mathbf C}:\mathbf D^{\text{op}}\times\mathbf C\to\mathbf C^{\text{op}}\times\mathbf C$.

**Definitions used.**

* In an opposite category $\mathbf A^{\text{op}}$, the objects are those of $\mathbf A$. Each morphism $X\to Y$ is $u^{\text{op}}$ for a unique morphism $u:Y\to X$ of $\mathbf A$. Composition is $v^{\text{op}}\circ_{\text{op}}u^{\text{op}}=(u\circ v)^{\text{op}}$ and identities are $\operatorname{id}_X^{\text{op}}$.
* A morphism $(X,Y)\to(X',Y')$ in a product category $\mathbf A\times\mathbf B$ is a pair $(a,b)$ with $a:X\to X'$ in $\mathbf A$ and $b:Y\to Y'$ in $\mathbf B$. Composition and identities are taken componentwise. For functors $F:\mathbf A\to\mathbf A'$ and $G:\mathbf B\to\mathbf B'$, the product functor $F\times G:\mathbf A\times\mathbf B\to\mathbf A'\times\mathbf B'$ is $(X,Y)\mapsto(FX,GY)$ and $(a,b)\mapsto(Fa,Gb)$.
* The hom bifunctor $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(-,-):\mathbf C^{\text{op}}\times\mathbf C\to\mathbf{Set}$ sends an object $(X,Y)$ to the set $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(X,Y)$, which is a set because $\mathbf C$ is locally small. A morphism $(u^{\text{op}},g):(X,Y)\to(X',Y')$, where $u:X'\to X$ and $g:Y\to Y'$ in $\mathbf C$, is sent to the mapping
$$\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(u,g):\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(X,Y)\to\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(X',Y'),\qquad h\mapsto g\circ h\circ u.$$
* The hom bifunctor with left functor $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(L-,-):\mathbf D^{\text{op}}\times\mathbf C\to\mathbf{Set}$ sends an object $(D,C)$ to $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(LD,C)$. A morphism $(f^{\text{op}},g):(D,C)\to(D',C')$, where $f:D'\to D$ in $\mathbf D$ and $g:C\to C'$ in $\mathbf C$, is sent to the mapping
$$\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(Lf,g):\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(LD,C)\to\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(LD',C'),\qquad h\mapsto g\circ h\circ Lf.$$
* A composite functor $G\circ F$ acts on objects by $X\mapsto G(FX)$ and on morphisms by $a\mapsto G(Fa)$.
* Two functors are equal when they have the same domain and the same codomain, agree on every object and agree on every morphism. Two morphisms of $\mathbf{Set}$ are equal when they have the same domain, the same codomain and the same value at every element.

**Step 1: $L^{\text{op}}$ and $L^{\text{op}}\times\operatorname{id}_{\mathbf C}$ are functors.**

Let $f^{\text{op}}:D\to D'$ in $\mathbf D^{\text{op}}$, so $f:D'\to D$ in $\mathbf D$. Then $Lf:LD'\to LD$, so $(Lf)^{\text{op}}:LD\to LD'$ in $\mathbf C^{\text{op}}$. Hence $L^{\text{op}}$ respects domains and codomains.

For identities: $L^{\text{op}}(\operatorname{id}_D^{\text{op}})=(L\operatorname{id}_D)^{\text{op}}=\operatorname{id}_{LD}^{\text{op}}$, which is the identity of $LD$ in $\mathbf C^{\text{op}}$.

For composition, take $f^{\text{op}}:D\to D'$ and $k^{\text{op}}:D'\to D''$. Then
$$L^{\text{op}}(k^{\text{op}}\circ_{\text{op}}f^{\text{op}})=L^{\text{op}}((f\circ k)^{\text{op}})=(L(f\circ k))^{\text{op}}=(Lf\circ Lk)^{\text{op}}=(Lk)^{\text{op}}\circ_{\text{op}}(Lf)^{\text{op}}=L^{\text{op}}(k^{\text{op}})\circ_{\text{op}}L^{\text{op}}(f^{\text{op}}).$$
So $L^{\text{op}}$ is a functor.

A product of functors is a functor, because identities and composition in a product category are componentwise. Hence $P:=L^{\text{op}}\times\operatorname{id}_{\mathbf C}:\mathbf D^{\text{op}}\times\mathbf C\to\mathbf C^{\text{op}}\times\mathbf C$ is a functor. Consequently $H:=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(-,-)\circ P$ is a well-defined functor from $\mathbf D^{\text{op}}\times\mathbf C$ to $\mathbf{Set}$. So $H$ has the same domain and the same codomain as $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(L-,-)$.

**Step 2: agreement on objects.**

Let $(D,C)$ be an object of $\mathbf D^{\text{op}}\times\mathbf C$. Then
$$H(D,C)=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(-,-)\big(L^{\text{op}}D,\operatorname{id}_{\mathbf C}C\big)=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(-,-)(LD,C)=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(LD,C)=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(L-,-)(D,C).$$

**Step 3: agreement on morphisms.**

Let $(f^{\text{op}},g):(D,C)\to(D',C')$ be any morphism of $\mathbf D^{\text{op}}\times\mathbf C$. Every morphism has this form, with $f:D'\to D$ in $\mathbf D$ uniquely determined and $g:C\to C'$ in $\mathbf C$. Applying $P$ gives
$$P(f^{\text{op}},g)=\big(L^{\text{op}}(f^{\text{op}}),\operatorname{id}_{\mathbf C}(g)\big)=\big((Lf)^{\text{op}},g\big):(LD,C)\to(LD',C'),$$
which is a morphism of $\mathbf C^{\text{op}}\times\mathbf C$ whose first component comes from $Lf:LD'\to LD$. By the definition of the hom bifunctor, applied with $X=LD$, $X'=LD'$, $u=Lf$, $Y=C$ and $Y'=C'$, the morphism $H(f^{\text{op}},g)$ is the mapping
$$\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(LD,C)\to\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(LD',C'),\qquad h\mapsto g\circ h\circ Lf.$$
The morphism $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(L-,-)(f^{\text{op}},g)$ is, by definition, a mapping with the same domain $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(LD,C)$ and the same codomain $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(LD',C')$. At every $h\in\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(LD,C)$ it takes the same value $g\circ h\circ Lf$. Hence the two are equal as morphisms of $\mathbf{Set}$:
$$H(f^{\text{op}},g)=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(L-,-)(f^{\text{op}},g).$$

**Conclusion.** The functors $H$ and $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(L-,-)$ have the same domain $\mathbf D^{\text{op}}\times\mathbf C$ and the same codomain $\mathbf{Set}$ (Step 1). They agree on all objects (Step 2) and on all morphisms (Step 3). Therefore
$$\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(L-,-)=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(-,-)\circ\big(L^{\text{op}}\times\operatorname{id}_{\mathbf C}\big).\qquad\blacksquare$$
